Into the *Thicket*

I finally got around to reading Aneesh's "Logic of the Thicket and the unsearchable web." There's lots of rich insights. 
https://aneeshsathe.com/logic-of-the-thicket-and-the-unsearchable-web/

A few initial reactions: 
- AI, like any statistical model, needs variation and information from which to find a central tendency. Homogenizing by moving ourselves into alignment with the machines. Flips the many common AI dogma on its head.[1]
- Cultivating the digital garden seems like a great start  but I also think that requires nurturing an ecosystem of diverse ideas IRL. A neighbor up the street built his own beautiful craftsman home. That type of creative act contributes to the interrelated diversity that Aneesh is talking about (at least in my understanding). That at least stands athwart the Airbnb-ification of everything.[2]
- On a secant, what are paths to nurture diversity of thought in an organization? A community? Another larger or smaller sized collection of humans (networked or otherwise)? What protocols should be implemented? 
- For a specific thought: What about a studio space for folks to reclaim their inner kid? To play and create and make? I am envisioning something like a digitally native chataqua, well actually that already exists. There are things like Edge Esmeralda doing pop up cities and making that type of creative community a reality. There are also other networks popping up. I wonder what it'd look like, not at the edge but at the center of existing communities. 
- Aneesh's thoughts on AI seem like a nice orthogonal to the dominant strains in the discourse that seem to be very much lacking. I do find the trader rather than guardian based ethic and pro-social curiousity to be quite a helpful line of inquiry. 

Looking at monikers for that different perspective on AI, I have been playing with the idea of the Qeng Ho, a space opera trading confederating in the far future of a piece of science fiction, as a motif for an alternative approach to AI beyond the boring accelerationists and doomers. (Those seem to be catnip for people who love to argue about clouds in the sky who've really dug into the dirt of the world.) 

[The Qeng Ho come from Vernor Vinge's *A Deepness in the Sky*. They are a loose network of merchant families crossing interstellar distances at slower-than-light speeds. A single trading run can take decades or centuries, so by the time a fleet arrives somewhere, the civilization it planned to trade with may have collapsed, recovered, or become something else. The Qeng Ho have seen this cycle of rise and fall on world after world, and their culture is built around surviving it. They don't conquer or rule. They carry knowledge, goods, and technical archives between worlds, and they make their living through exchange and long-term reputation. Being useful to whoever happens to be in charge is what keeps them in business, generation after generation.

Their relationship to technology is the part I find most interesting. It isn't sleek or magical. Their ships run on software stacks thousands of years deep, layer on layer of code written by people long dead, much of it patched, wrapped, and repurposed over and over. One of the most valued roles in the fleet is essentially a programmer-archaeologist: someone who digs through that sediment to understand why things work and how to bend them to new problems. Technology here is less an engine of transcendence and more a craft tradition. It's inherited, maintained, traded, and slowly tended over time.

That shapes how they think about AI. In Vinge's universe, the big dreams of strong, self-improving machine intelligence (along with faster-than-light travel and a few others) are known as "Failed Dreams." People have chased them over and over, and in the Qeng Ho's part of the galaxy they reliably don't pan out. So the Qeng Ho don't hand themselves over to a superintelligence, and they don't spend their days fearing one either. Their automation is everywhere and very capable, but it's woven into human skill and judgment. The machines are tools and partners in the work of keeping a fleet alive and trading. They aren't gods to be summoned or monsters to be contained.

That's why they work as a motif for me. The Qeng Ho stance is basically the trader ethic Aneesh describes. It's pragmatic, curious, and oriented toward exchange with many different peoples rather than one final destination. It assumes a world that stays plural and messy, and it treats technology as something you cultivate over the long haul instead of something that either saves or ends everything. It also gets value from difference: a trader only has something to offer if the worlds they travel between stay distinct from one another.]

***

[1] Another sci fi connection: [- I keep thinking about the Ousters from Dan Simmons' *Hyperion* books. The Hegemony of Man is comfortable and interconnected: farcaster portals stitch hundreds of worlds into one seamless network, and the AIs of the TechnoCore run nearly everything. Everyone lives in roughly the same culture, wired into the same datasphere, and the Hegemony calls the Ousters barbarians. The Ousters are humans who stayed out of the web and went off to live in the dark between stars. Over generations they adapted themselves to space: zero-g bodies, vacuum skin, kilometers-wide wings to catch sunlight, whole floating forests for habitats. The twist is that the Hegemony's convenience was the trap. Its integration with the Core made it dependent and, in the end, harvestable, while the Ousters' refusal to plug in left them free to keep becoming something new. That's Aneesh's thicket in story form. The smooth, searchable, fully aligned network turns out to be a monoculture, and the messy, illegible, divergent fringe is where humanity keeps its capacity to evolve. For us, cultivating that diversity probably means making room for our own little Ouster swarms: people, places, and practices that stay deliberately off the main grid, odd and hard to index. They shouldn't be treated as backwardness to be absorbed. They're the reservoir of variation everything else, AI included, ultimately depends on.]

[2] [- The flip side of my neighbor's house is what Kyle Chayka named "AirSpace": the look that spread across coffee shops, co-working spaces, and short-term rentals in the 2010s. Reclaimed wood, white subway tile, Edison bulbs, mid-century furniture, a fiddle-leaf fig in the corner, open shelving, minimal clutter. A café in Brooklyn starts to look like one in Seoul, Berlin, or Buenos Aires.

  Nobody planned it. Airbnb listings, Instagram, Pinterest, and Foursquare rewarded spaces that photographed well and felt familiar to a mobile, globally connected class of travelers and remote workers. Hosts and owners noticed what got booked, liked, and reviewed, and they copied it. Platforms like Airbnb then pushed the convergence further with photography services, design guides, and ranking signals.

  The result is comfortable and frictionless. It is also placeless, because local character gets sanded off in favor of whatever the feedback loop rewards. It's the physical-world version of what Aneesh is warning about: people aligning themselves to the algorithm's central tendency until the variation the system depends on starts to disappear. A hand-built craftsman house is a small act of resistance against that.

  Chayka's original piece is still the clearest summary: https://www.theverge.com/2016/8/3/12325104/airbnb-aesthetic-global-minimalism-startup-gentrification. The Longreads take is here: https://longreads.com/2017/05/18/airbnb-design-aesthetic/]
